column1: Place an Upper Limit on the Number of Fandoms a Tag Wrangler Can Assign Themselves
column11: This is the project to use for issues related to Archive of Our Own.
column27:
To date Tag Wranglers have no hard limit in regards to the number of fandoms they can assign themselves. Recently, however, we altered our Assigned Fandoms Policy to limit the number of fandoms any individual wrangler can assign themselves to 450 fandoms. As this limit is in place and this policy is active and in force fully as of the end of April, we would like to make this a hard limit within the system to avoid this being something that needs to be checked and managed by TW Supervisors or Chairs. 

*PLEASE NOTE:* We do not plan on this limit changing frequently. As such, this should be a config rather than an admin setting.

h1. Expected Behavior:

When a wrangler attempts to assign themselves to more than 450 fandoms, they should receive the following message, where %{count} is the number of fandoms they currently wrangler:

{quote}You currently wrangle %{count} fandoms. Please de-assign any fandom(s) you are no longer interested in wrangling before attempting to assign yourself to additional fandoms. {quote}

Wranglers who already wrangle over 450 fandoms when the change is made should 

* be able to wrangle as usual
* be able to de-assign fandoms one at a time

Additionally, the wrangling pages ({{/tag_wranglers/USERNAME}}) for individual wranglers should have the following text added to the paragraph that contains the last wrangling date:

{quote}%{username}  is currently wrangling %{count} Fandoms.{quote}

This information should be available to the wrangler the page belongs to and any admins who can access the page, but not to other wranglers. (In other words, there’s no need to change the [existing logic|https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/blob/19d32d9aa73615509c222a443b20e1ec2347595c/app/views/tag_wranglers/show.html.erb#L26] around that paragraph.)

h1. Testing Instructions (Once Limitation is in Place):

Required: Tag Wrangler Role

# Go to the Wranglers page and assign yourself to 450 fandoms. The quickest way to do this is by grabbing a list of 450 fandoms (or if you already have some fandoms assigned, whatever number gets you there), insert commas between each of the fandom names, copy that list and paste it into the box at the top of the screen. Click the “Assign” button. This will assign you to ever fandom in the list. 
# Attempt to assign yourself to another fandom. This can be done via the Sign Up link on any unwrangled fandom page, the text box at the top of the Wranglers page or via the drop down boxes below fandoms displayed on the Wranglers page. Please try all three methods.
# All methods should return an error message: You currently wrangle %{count} fandoms. Please de-assign any fandom(s) you are no longer interested in wrangling before attempting to assign yourself to additional fandoms. 
# De-assign a fandom and confirm you can pick up another fandom. 
# Go to your wrangling page ({{/tag_wranglers/USERNAME}}) and confirm it now has the following in the same paragraph as the last wrangled information: %{username} is currently wrangling %{count} Fandoms.
# Go to another wrangler’s wrangling page and confirm the previous information is not present for you.

Required: Admin with superadmin or tag_wrangling role

# Go to a wrangler’s wrangling page ({{/tag_wranglers/USERNAME}}) and confirm it now has the following in the same paragraph as the last wrangled information: %{username} is currently wrangling %{count} Fandoms.

column1: Collections: Updated date in blurbs not displaying in correct timezone
column11: This is the project to use for issues related to Archive of Our Own.
column27:
h2. Steps to Reproduce

# Log in
# Go to your preferences and set your time zone to GMT+13.
# Create a new collection
# Wait a few minutes
# View the collection blurb on [https://test.archiveofourown.org/collections|https://test.archiveofourown.org/collections] and take note of the date that is shown in the blurb in the top right
# Go to your preferences and set your time zone to GMT-12
# Create a new collection
# Wait a few minutes
# View the collection blurbs on [https://test.archiveofourown.org/collections|https://test.archiveofourown.org/collections] and take note of the dates that are shown in the blurbs

h2. What happens

The collection that you created first appears to have been created the day after the collection you  created second. This is because the collections' last updated date is displayed in the current user’s time zone, and then cached. So the first collection’s date is displayed in GMT+13, and the second collection’s date is displayed in GMT-12 – apparently 1 day earlier, even though the collection was actually updated later.

h2. What should happen

When you change your time zone, the collection blurb’s date should be displayed in your new time zone.

h2. Development notes

In [https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-7337|https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-7337|smart-link]  the collection blurb cache was separated into multiple parts to solve this same issue for the sign-up closing time. We can rearrange these cache parts so that they also do not include the updated date for the collection.

For performance reasons, please do not create more cache parts, but instead move their starts/ends around in the blurb so that the updated_at is excluded. You may also want to reevaluate whether all the cache keys need to include the logged_in status. If you change the cache key names, consider changing them to the array format instead of manually concatenating, e.g. {{cache([:v1, :collection_blurb, :heading, collection.id], expires_in: ....)}}.

We want to follow a similar flow to the one established in [https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-6918|https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-6918|smart-link], with a few modifications:

# The links to setup two-step verification, disable two-step verifiation, and regenerate backup codes should go on the preferences page ([http://archiveofourown.org/users/USERNAME/preferences|http://archiveofourown.org/users/USERNAME/preferences]) in a new section. Refer to the attached image for further information.
# The copy button from [https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-7359|https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-7359|smart-link] should be included in the user two-step verification setup workflow.
# The copy button from [https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-7378|https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-7378|smart-link]  should also be included.

h1. Deploy notes

* Has pre-deploy migration: {{rails db:migrate:up VERSION=XXXXXXXXXX}}
* Deploy
* Needs a worker restart

h1. Testing

# Log in as a regular user and go to your preferences age.
# Verify you can access the link to enable two-step verification and that the status is reported as disabled.
# Follow the link to enable two-step verification.
## Try entering an incorrect password to make sure you can’t proceed.
## Enter the correct password to make sure you can proceed.
# On the page to enable two-step verification, copy the string of letters/numbers near the QR code.
## Follow [https://support.1password.com/one-time-passwords|https://support.1password.com/one-time-passwords|smart-link]  to setup this in 1password. (If you have a preferred two-factor authentication app, feel free to use that instead.)
## Copy the 6-digit code from 1password (or your 2fa app) and use it to confirm two-step verification enablement.
## Save the backup codes that you are now shown.
# Log out of your account.
# Log in again.
## Make sure you can log in with the 6-digit code _currently shown_ in 1password or your authenticator app.
## Log out.
# Log in again.
## Try using one of your backup codes instead when prompted for a two-step verification code.
## Log out, then try to log in with the same code. You should not be able to.
## Try to log in using another backup code. This one should work.
# Follow the link to regenerate backup codes, and repeat step 7 with the new codes.
# Log out and make sure you can request a password reset for your admin account and reset your password without being prompted for two-step verification.
# Make sure you can disable two-step verification and then log in without providing a code.

18/May/26 9:07 AM;60d5d58e8f2cc10069d7e879;Since this feature is targeted for users, I think we should probably put more focus on improving the UX:

# Should we add a step before step 1 and tell the user to set up an authenticator app on their phone? eg. give them specific instructions for both Android and iOS.
# Unlike the admin side, users might try to set up 2FA while using the browser on their phone. I’ve added a {{otpauth://}} link button under the “Setup on This Device” heading for that scenario.
# I think we should add a hint saying “Scan with your authenticator app” under the QR code. I have a feeling some users will use their camera app otherwise.
# Should we make it more clear that when they re-generate their backup codes, the old copies will stop working?
# Should we automatically disable 2FA whenever a recovery code is used? 

!image-20260518-152934.png|width=692,alt="image-20260518-152934.png"!

There’s also some security design questions:

# Should we send emails to notify users when they set up or disable 2FA?
# For password reset requests, should we allow users to reset their password without putting in their 2FA code? I know the current plan is to allow this, but I think this is a bit unconventional.
# Should we allow users to change their email address/password/disable 2FA/re-generate backup codes/delete their account while logged-in without putting in their 2FA code?

I guess these would depend on the threat model. Is the threat model to prevent password leaks on other sites leading to account loss (ie. blocking at logins only) or something a bit more advanced, like a sibling or parent with access to a shared computer?
column132: 18/May/26 9:47 AM;60d5d58e8f2cc10069d7e879;Oh and there's also the question for admin intervention & the associated role scoping. column1: Strip punctuation from guest names before comparing against banned usernames list
column11: This is the project to use for issues related to Archive of Our Own.
column27:
In [https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-6040|https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-6040|smart-link] we prevented guest comments using names that matched a predetermined list of banned usernames. 

Because guest names have a much wider range of allowed characters than registered usernames, we should use regex to strip whitespace and punctuation before comparing the entered name to the banned username list. 

We should also strip underscores before comparing registered usernames against the banned username list, which will allow us to remove additional duplicate entries from the current list post-deploy.

If possible, it would be nice to account for common substitutions/easily confused characters (diacritics, lowercase L vs uppercase I, numeral 0 and letter O, Cyrillic А vs Latin A, etc).

{noformat}
Looking through the traces, my overall picture is that you are over-using cache, peppering sometimes hundreds of cache calls all over the place. I can see how you got here. You're trying to remove load from the SQL database and put it somewhere else. But from the perspective of total latency of the entire transaction, you haven't improved things much (Redis isn't magically faster than a hot, in-the-buffers hit from a MySQL db).

If you look at, for example, `_intro_module.html.erb`, there's several cache calls happening right in a row.

I think this could be improved by focusing less on `Rails.cache` manual usage, but instead focusing on more cache (and cache-reuse) of entire HTML fragments at the view layer. You're caching _more_ activity (not just the query but also the HTML generation) and also across potentially _multiple_ queries and datasources.

Another example: on the homepage, for each marked for later work, there are 5 cache round trips to render the blurb, even though the fragment itself is already cached. If the entire readings section was single fragment keyed per-user, you could turn 30 cache ops into 1.{noformat}

column1: Change send_data to a background job powered workflow
column11: This is the project to use for issues related to Archive of Our Own.
column27:
You have a couple places in the codebase where you're using {{send_data}} to send files of fairly significant size down to the client:

# *DownloadsController#show*
# *send_csv_data* helper, used by ChallengeSignupsController, TagWranglers controller, AdminUsers controller.

There are two big issues with what's happening here.

* *Memory usage*. You're loading ~several mb of stuff into memory at once to put some of these CSVs together. In a web process, that memory usage sticks around and is difficult to get rid of. In a background process, usually this kind of "dirtiness" in the heap is already occurring so you're not making things much worse, and it's in general easier to stop and restart background job processes.
* *Transmitting large files to the client is slow* Ruby web servers aren't really designed for this. Puma does not buffer client responses and so you're essentially locking up the thread for as long as it takes to stream this response back to the client. It's worse for single-threaded situations (which you're in I think, for web today).

Both of these I think could get out of hand and cause some minor incidents.

For me, the best path forward would be to reorient the whole thing around a background job:

# Controller kicks off a job to generate the CSV.
# Controller returns to the web client a URL and says "your CSV will be here when it's done".
# Background job does the CSV work and uploads to S3.
# S3 serves the CSV.

This would solve both problems for you at once. You could optionally try to work to stream the CSV upload as well to reduce memory usage in the worker, but honestly I think just getting it out of the web process is enough.

column1: Remove puma_worker_killer, after verifying no leaks
column11: This is the project to use for issues related to Archive of Our Own.
column27:
ou have {{puma_worker_killer}} in the {{Gemfile}}. There's no other config in the gem for it, but this gem is frequently configured with env variables.

PWK's job is to {{SIGTERM}} processes which go over a particular memory threshold. This sounds like a nice-to-have "safety" feature, but it's a footgun in waiting.

Several years ago I was consulting on a client project and the app was just really slow. I was looking at the response times and thinking, this app is about twice as slow as it probably should be. What's going on? We removed {{puma_worker_killer}} and watched response times drop in half instantly.

It turned out that someone had installed and configured {{puma_worker_killer}} years ago and had forgotten about it. As the app grew over time, it continued to _work_, but the baseline memory usage of the app just kept increasing, leading to more and more frequent process restarts triggered by {{puma_worker_killer}}. In the end, it turned out Puma processes were processing about 20 requests on average before being restarted.

Old processes are fast processes. We want processes to stick around for as long as possible.

{{puma_worker_killer}} combines two things which are almost always _very difficult_ to observe as an SRE:

# Configuration in ENV variables. ENV variables are almost always forgotten about. No one knows what they are and what they are set to, because they often contain secrets. Access to them is restricted as a result, and they're not easily checked or in the front of anyone's mind.
# The "failure mode" is high process restarts, which is almost never properly observed. If PWK's thresholds are set too low, the only way you're going to find out is if you look at how often process restarts are happening and think: hm, that's a bit high (which, you may not even realize after looking at it). Your app could be restarting _after serving only a single request_ and you might not notice it, if load is low enough and you've provisioned enough puma processes.

{{puma_worker_killer}} is sort of a relic from a Heroku-dominant era, where you needed to fit processes into teeny-tiny dynos of like 512MB. Nowadays, most people buy cloud hardware with 4GB of RAM per CPU, and an application which cannot fit within that constraint reliably is far more sick than something {{puma_worker_killer}} can even address.

For that reason, I think {{puma_worker_killer}} should be removed from the setup.

column1: Use Prosopite to test/remove N+1s
column11: This is the project to use for issues related to Archive of Our Own.
column27:
I've never been all that high on Bullet, but recently I've had a lot of success with [prosopite|https://github.com/charkost/prosopite]. It's highly accurate, with basically zero false positives. That means you can set up a workflow where Prosopite is configured to {{raise}} by default in the test environment. That means you can't ship new features with proven N+1s! That's an extremely powerful thing to be always checking for in the background without any additional effort.

Usually what I do with clients is work along the following axis:

# Install prosopite, log in dev and test.
# Add prosopite as an RSpec context tag, like {{:check_for_n_plus_ones}}. Add it to all test classes which don't have N+1s in them today (add them everywhere they wouldn't fail a test today).
# Gradually burn through the remaining bad examples/classes, adding the context one by one, until you have just a few left. At that point, you can...
# Make prosopite {{raise}} by default in test and remove the remaining N+1s as global ignores in prosopite's config.

It's extremely useful!

column1: Preload roles on the user details page for admins
column11: This is the project to use for issues related to Archive of Our Own.
column27:
I noticed a lot of Sentry traces with {{roles}} lookups peppered all over the place. You already do the right thing in {{permit_yo}}:

{code:ruby}def has_role?(role_name)
  return self.roles.any? { |role| role.name == role_name.to_s } if self.roles.loaded?

  role = Role.find_by(name: role_name)
  self.roles.include?(role)
end{code}

So that's good. The fact that these queries are happening then is a sign that the association wasn't {{loaded}}.

I've encountered this permissions thing a ton of times. I think it's almost always worth it to just load all user roles upfront rather than try to be clever about which you load when.

Since you're using Devise, you override {{serialize_from_session}}:

{code:ruby}def self.serialize_from_session(key, salt)
  record = includes(:roles).where(primary_key => key).first
  record if record && record.authenticatable_salt == salt
end{code}

There are also a handful of places in views where you inspect {{user.roles}} directly, e.g. {{@user.roles.any?}}. I'd replace all these with {{has_role?}} and then make sure the association is loaded.

column27:
Of course _I'm_ gonna say this, as I'm the maintainer. But I really do think it's a great application server! It looks like you're about halfway to transitioning.

Moving from single-threaded Unicorn to single-threaded Puma should just be a "straight swap". When you use the servers in this way they don't really differ that much in terms of behavior.

I think probably this application never becomes multi-threaded. It's probably just more hassle than it's worth. I usually tell people: what changing your concurrency model gives you (from processes to threads, threads to fibers, etc) is allows you to run more open, idle connections with low switching cost and low memory use. If your workload doesn't have that need, process based concurrency probably works just fine for you. Almost every major Rails app, the real giga-shops like Shopify, Github, Intercom, Gusto: they're all running single-threaded. They decided the threading bugs aren't worth the ~30% memory savings. I suspect, given the limited volunteer resources and the age of this app, that the calculus is the same for you.

# {{active_record_query_trace}} gem. Appends a colorized multi-line call stack after each query in dev logs.
# {{config.active_record.verbose_query_logs}} = true.  Rails 5.2+ built-in, appends ↳ file:line after each query
# {{config/initializers/active_record_log_subscriber.rb}} — a custom LogQuerySource module that also prepends ↳ file:line

While I love this feature and of course recommend everyone use it, it is kinda baked into Rails now and I prefer to use the Rails mainline stuff where I can rather than bring in dependencies. Probably we only need one of these right?

It is a little bit of a bummer but verbose_query_logs only displays a single line:

User Load (0.4ms)  SELECT "users".* FROM "users" WHERE ...

## View the first work’s notes

## View the first work’s notes
## Download the first work and view the download

14/Jun/26 8:52 AM;70121:ef9b850c-da94-4131-9e12-6dd30489e7ab;As a complement, this full edited text for the pop up: {noformat}

Matching

The matching process for gift exchanges runs in two stages:

Potential Matching
All the sign-ups are compared and for each person we generate a list of potential givers (people who can give them a gift), and potential recipients (people they can give a gift to). This is the slowest part of the process and can take as much as a day for a very large challenge or one where almost all the participants match each other.
Assignments
We try to give everyone a single assignment, starting with the people who have the fewest potential givers or recipients and working up until no one else can be assigned. This process is relatively fast; it generally completes within an hour.

You may have to decide how to fix several issues that can come up during matching.

Potential Match Issues

Invalid Sign-ups

Sometimes a challenge can end up with one or more invalid sign-ups -- duplicates, or sign-ups that have too many or too few offers/requests or ones that don't fit the rules of your challenge. Most commonly, this happens if someone clicks submit or update multiple times because their connection to the archive is slow. It can also happen if you have changed the rules of your challenge partway through the sign-up process -- read further for details about this.

If this happens, potential matching won't run, and you'll be quickly emailed a list of links to the invalid sign-ups so you can examine them. You can often tell easily when two sign-ups or offers/requests are duplicates, in which case you can just delete the duplicates. Sometimes you may have to contact a participant to figure out which of the sign-ups or prompts they want to use.

If on the other hand you made the rules more strict mid-stream and you have a large number of invalid sign-ups as a result, you may only be able to fix this by easing your rules to match the lowest common denominator. For instance, if you started by requiring 2 offers and 2 requests, and then upped the requirement to 3 offers and 3 requests a day into sign-up, you may have a whole slew of sign-ups that only have 2/2 and are now therefore considered invalid. To fix this, you'll have to change your challenge settings back to only requiring 2/2, while allowing 3/3.

After you have dealt with all the invalid sign-ups, you can then start matching again.

No matches

If you have no potential matches, there are a few things you can do:

First, make sure that your gift exchange's Minimum Number to Match settings are set correctly. If they are set too high, then matching may not work.

If you're still having issues, check your gift exchange's sign-ups. If none of the sign-ups match with each other, you may need to contact participants and ask if there are more things they're willing to create or receive.

You can also change the Minimum Number to Match settings to 0 and assign matches manually.

For more information, check out What is matching and how do I complete the process in my Gift Exchange?, or the Matching section in our tutorial, Running a Gift Exchange on AO3.

column1: Disallow enabling a locale for the interface if it can't be used for emails
column11: This is the project to use for issues related to Archive of Our Own.
column27:
h2. Steps to reproduce

# Log in as an admin with the {{superadmin}} or {{translation}} role
# Follow “Locales” in the admin nav bar
# Press “Edit” for a locale that has “User for Email” set to false
# Check “Use this locale for the interface”
# Press “Update Locale”

h2. What happens

The locale is successfully updated.

h2. What should happen

Updating the locale should fail with an error “Use for interface can only be enabled if use for emails is also enabled.”. We want this to error because locales that don’t have translated emails definitely won’t have a translated interface, so we don’t want to accidentally have the translated interface enabled for them.

h2. Notes

There are currently no locales in this state on production or staging, so we do not need a rake task to fix them.

Diversity Statement

You are welcome at the Archive of Our Own (AO3).

AO3 is a permanent, panfandom archive for fanworks, built by fans, for fans. We want AO3 to be a place where all fannish works are recognized as legal and transformative, and where every fan of any media feels welcome, no matter who they are or how they use AO3. If you enjoy creating or engaging with fanworks, AO3 is for you.

We take our commitment to maximum inclusiveness of fanwork content seriously. Our content policies are designed to give creators as much creative freedom as possible, while still allowing us to maintain our focus as a non-commercial fanwork archive. We strive to protect your rights to privacy and free expression, as outlined in our Terms of Service.

We value making fannish activities and creations as accessible as possible to all those who wish to participate. We recognize that supporting diversity and inclusion is an ongoing responsibility, and we remain dedicated to developing AO3 and its policies in a way that reflects our commitment. As we update AO3, we will continue to prioritize features that improve the site's inclusivity and accessibility for everyone.

We dedicate our time to support AO3, but we can't do this work alone. All of us – donors, users, and volunteers – work together to foster a culture of inclusiveness on AO3 and the rest of the Organization for Transformative Works' projects.

AO3 exists to support fans, fandoms, and fanworks of all kinds, and we welcome your feedback on how to make that possible.

We’d like to update the About page [https://test.archiveofourown.org/about|https://test.archiveofourown.org/about] to include information about AO3, not just OTW. {noformat}

About AO3 and the OTW

About AO3

The Archive of Our Own (AO3) is a non-profit, non-commercial fanwork archive for transformative fanworks; created by and for fans of books, music, art, games, shows, movies, real-person fiction (RPF), and other fandoms.

AO3 is built upon the principle of maximum inclusiveness of fanwork content. Fanworks that do not violate the Content Policy or some other part of the Terms of Service will not be removed from AO3, even if someone believes they are offensive or objectionable.

AO3 runs on open-source archiving software developed by the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW). Anyone is welcome to contribute by working on the unclaimed tasks in our Jira project.

AO3 entered open beta in November 2009 and exited beta in April 2026. You can read more about AO3's history on Fanlore.

Our Team

Behind the scenes, AO3 is run by volunteers serving on committees, which collaborate to support AO3 in different ways:

  • Accessibility, Design, & Technology designs, maintains, and develops AO3's code.
  • AO3 Documentation creates and maintains AO3's FAQs, help pop-ups, and tutorials.
  • Communications publishes news posts on AO3 and communicates with users about AO3-related updates.
  • Open Doors imports at-risk archives and fanzines to AO3.
  • Policy & Abuse addresses questions and reports about potential violations of the AO3 Terms of Service.
  • Support helps users resolve technical problems and passes on user feedback to other AO3 committees.
  • Systems manages the servers that AO3 runs on.
  • Tag Wrangling sorts and organizes tags on AO3, linking related tags together for better filtering and searching.
  • Translation helps committees communicate with users in non-English languages and translates news and information about AO3.
  • User Response Translation addresses Policy & Abuse and Support's translation needs in specific high-need languages.

About the OTW

The OTW is a 501(c)(3) non-profit organization, fully supported by donations and run by and for fans. The OTW's mission is to preserve and protect transformative fanworks and fan culture in their myriad forms. We believe that fanworks are transformative and that transformative works are legitimate.

Our other major projects include:

  • Fanlore, a fandom wiki devoted to preserving the history of transformative fanworks and the fandoms from which they have arisen. Visit Fanlore.
  • Legal Advocacy, which is committed to protecting and defending fanworks from commercial exploitation and legal challenges. They also strive to educate fans about developments in law that could affect fandom.
  • Open Doors, which offers shelter to at-risk fannish projects and archives. Through several subprojects, they preserve different kinds of fanworks and artifacts of fan culture. Visit Open Doors.
  • Transformative Works and Cultures (TWC), an international, peer-reviewed journal that publishes articles about transformative works and fan communities. Visit TWC.

Learn More

You can find information on using AO3 in the Archive FAQs, or visit the OTW FAQs to learn more about our organization. If you want to get involved, you can Donate or Volunteer.

For technical help using AO3, including bug reports and feature requests, please contact Support. For questions or reports about violations of the AO3 Terms of Service, contact Policy & Abuse. If you have any other questions, please contact Communications.

After [https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-7442|https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-7442|smart-link] is in place, users will be able to authenticate with a two-step verification (AKA two-factor authentication) code or backup code. Bump the [net-imap gem|https://github.com/ruby/net-imap] from 0.5.14 to 0.5.15 to resolve several vulnerabilites: 

* [https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8p34-64r3-mwg8|https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8p34-64r3-mwg8|smart-link] 
* [https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-46q3-7gv7-qmgg|https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-46q3-7gv7-qmgg|smart-link] 
* [https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c4fp-cxrr-mj66|https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c4fp-cxrr-mj66|smart-link] 

*Testing*

We don’t receive/retrieve any emails with IMAP. However, the gem is a dependency of actionmailer, so let’s do a smoke test that sending emails still works.

# Press “Save changes”

h2. What happens

You get at least the following errors:

* Name can only be changed by an admin.
* Name can't be blank
* Name cannot be blank.
* Tag name '' cannot include the following restricted characters: , ^ * < > { } = ` ， 、 \ %

h2. What should happen

You should not get the last error, because the tag name is empty, so it doesn’t contain those characters. You also shouldn’t get two error messages about the name being blank. The other error(s) is/are fine.

h2. Notes

This happens because the format validation for the characters uses {{with}} and a regex with a negated set, instead of using {{without}} and a non-negated set. The duplicated blank error happens due there being validations for both the name’s presence and the name’s minimum length. Based on the [Rails guide|https://guides.rubyonrails.org/active_record_validations.html#length] we should remove the length validation, as the presence validation already handles 0 length tags.

column1: Backfill task for users missing username-matching pseud
column11: This is the project to use for issues related to Archive of Our Own.
column27:
After [https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-6359|https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-6359|smart-link], it is no longer possible for a user to delete the pseud that corresponds to their username; however, we have a couple hundred users for whom this is the case, and several hundred more users whose matching pseud actually differs in capitalization or diacritics (e.g., a user with the login “Name” and a pseud “name” or “Näme”). 

To make sure everyone has a pseud that matches their username exactly, we want an {{After}} rake task that backfills a default pseud or updates the partially-matching pseud for these users.

Roughly, this looks like

{code:ruby}user = ...
pseud = Pseud.new(user_id: user.id, name: user.login)
pseud.save!{code}

One query I’ve come up with to find these users (needs converting to Ruby and there may be more efficient ways):

{code:sql}SELECT * FROM users WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pseuds WHERE name = users.login LIMIT 1);{code}

h1. Testing

# As a database admin, find the pseud matching a user’s login and delete it. (Validation will likely need to be bypassed).
# Confirm as the user that the pseud is no longer shown in your manage pseuds page.
# Run the rake task.
# Refresh the page (and perhaps wait a bit for caching) to make sure the pseud now shows up again.

h1. Deploy notes

This has an after task: {{bundle exec rake After:backfill_missing_pseuds}}

column1: Disable phone number detection in emails on iOS
column11: This is the project to use for issues related to Archive of Our Own.
column27:
iOS Mail interprets numerical strings of certain lengths as phone numbers. This can cause the numerical string to be converted to a link in places like word counts and summaries in subscription emails, and comment text in comment emails. 

To prevent this, we should add the following meta tag to the [HTML email template|https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/blob/master/app/views/layouts/mailer.html.erb]: 

{{<meta name="format-detection" content="telephone=no">}}

h1. Testing

You’ll need to open an email in iOS’s Mail app. This template is used for all emails, so you only need to test one of the following:

# A subscription email for a work with more than a million words
# A subscription email for a work with a numerical string like 8675309 or 555-2657 in the summary.
# A comment email with a numerical string like 8675309 or 555-2657 in the summary.

Note that the comment email is probably easiest, since it does not have a delay. 

Regardless of which email you test, the numbers should not be converted into a link and should instead appear as plain text.

column1: Remove active URL validation for external works
column11: This is the project to use for issues related to Archive of Our Own.
column27:
An increasing number of sites block requests from AO3’s servers, e.g. due to general bot access prevention measures. In the past we’ve allowlisted specific sites to be used for external works to work around this, such as [https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-7129|https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-7129|smart-link].

At this point adding exceptions for all sites that block us is becoming infeasible due to the number of sites that would need to be allowlisted. Additionally, the validation was likely created to mark links dead if they were unreachable, which we no longer do: [https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-6314|https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-6314|smart-link]. This means the validation no longer fulfills its intended purpose.

So lets just remove the {{url_active}} validation and associated {{UrlActiveValidator}} completely. (There’s also a comment in {{UrlFormatValidator}} that will need updating.)

h2. Testing instructions

# Log in
# Browse > Bookmarks > Bookmark External Work
# Fill “[https://www.reddit.com/|https://www.reddit.com/]” into the URL field
# Fill in the rest of the required fields
# Press “Create”

h2. What happens

You get an error that “Url could not be reached. If the URL is correct and the site is currently down, please try again later.”

h2. What should happen

The bookmark should save.

Other testing URLs that are always unreachable should also be bookmarkable: {{http://foo.invalid}}, {{http://foo.test/}}

column1: Creator comment cache not expired when creatorships of anonymous work change
column11: This is the project to use for issues related to Archive of Our Own.
column27:
h2. Steps to reproduce

# Post a work with a co-creator in an anonymous collection
# Log in as the co-creator and accept the co-creator request
# As the original user from step 1, comment on your own work
# Open the comment in another tab using the “Thread” button
# Observe that your comment is listed as being by “Anonymous Creator” since the work is anon
# Remove yourself as the co-creator
## Navigate to the work
## Press “Edit”
## Press “Remove Me As Co-Creator” and confirm
# Refresh the tab with the comment

h2. What happens

The comment is still anonymous, showing as being made by “Anonymous Creator”.

h2. What should happen

Since you’re no longer a co-creator on the work, the comment should be de-anonymized and show your username.

Conversely, if the co-creator adds you back to the work and you accept the co-creatorship request, all comments you left on the work should be re-anonymized.

column1: Rspec requests tests fail if run directly after other tests that use Elasticsearch
column11: This is the project to use for issues related to Archive of Our Own.
column27:
Some tests in {{spec/requests}} rely on Elasticsearch indexes existing, however the test definitions don’t specify this. This means that if a test that _does_ specify that it requires Elasticsearch, e.g. {{spec/controllers/fandoms_controller_spec.rb}} with {{work_search: true}}, is run before the requests specs, that test ends up destroying the Elasticsearch index afterwards, and the requests specs no longer have access to them and fail.

This problem doesn’t show up in our automated test runs on GitHub because controllers, models and requests specs are run separately. However, we’d like to support running them after each other in any desired order for local development.

To fix this bug, the requests specs that require Elasticsearch should specify that, using {{collection_search: true}},  {{work_search: true}} etc as applicable, to make sure the required indexes exist.

h2. Testing

In a local dev environment, run the following command to run tests in an order that was affected by this bug:

{noformat}bundle exec rspec spec/controllers/challenge_requests_controller_spec.rb spec/models/search/user_indexer_spec.rb spec/models/search/pseud_indexer_spec.rb spec/requests{noformat}

The tests should all pass. It should be enough if just one person tests this.

column27:
We need to include two additional parameters in our comment spam-check API requests to improve detection accuracy.

h2. Requirements

* _permalink_ — The URL of the AO3 page the user is commenting on.
**  Use the specific domain the user is on (e.g. [archiveofourown.org|http://archiveofourown.org] vs archiveofourown.gay), not always .org. Akismet said this provides the best context.
** Include the path when available (e.g. {{/works/:id/chapters/:id}}) to reflect the exact page the user was on.
* _blog_lang_ — Language code of the submission (work/admin post) being commented on (e.g. blog_lang=ru, blog_lang=en)
** If the language is unknown, omit blog_lang entirely.

h2. Testing

Make sure you can leave a guest comment on a work in English (which would be submitted with blog_lang) and in Aardvarkish (which is a made-up language and would be omitted).

h2. Steps to reproduce

## Post > New Work

# Hide the work

Listing a protected user’s work as inspiration: fails with an error message saying “You can't use the related works function to cite works by the protected user [name].”

column1: Redirect in check_modify_parent method of CommentController assumes drafts are works
column11: This is the project to use for issues related to Archive of Our Own.
column27:
Now that admin posts can be drafts, we need to update the redirect (and code comment) in CommentController’s [check_modify_parent method|https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/blob/45ab45c0429514ff367bcc31b321cce98d8fb312/app/controllers/comments_controller.rb#L112-L130]:

{code:ruby}  def check_modify_parent
    parent = find_parent
    # No one can create or update comments on something hidden by an admin.
    if parent.respond_to?(:hidden_by_admin) && parent.hidden_by_admin
      flash[:error] = ts("Sorry, you can't add or edit comments on a hidden work.")
      redirect_to work_path(parent)
    end
    # No one can create or update comments on unrevealed works.
    if parent.respond_to?(:in_unrevealed_collection) && parent.in_unrevealed_collection
      flash[:error] = ts("Sorry, you can't add or edit comments on an unrevealed work.")
      redirect_to work_path(parent)
    end

    # No one can create or update comments on unpublished (A.K.A. unposted) works.
    return unless parent.respond_to?(:posted) && !parent.posted

    flash[:error] = t("comments.check_modify_parent.draft")
    redirect_to work_path(parent)
  end{code}

That last {{redirect_to work_path(parent)}} will send you to the work with the ID of the news post draft instead of the news post. 

h1. Testing

This can just be tested with an automated test. (I only found it because I had commented out the [line preventing users from accessing draft news posts|https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/blob/45ab45c0429514ff367bcc31b321cce98d8fb312/app/controllers/admin_posts_controller.rb#L23].)

column27:
h1. Steps to reproduce

# Log in
# Create a work skin
## Hi, Username! > My Dashboard > Skins > My Work Skins > Create Work Skin
## Fill in a unique title
## Fill in some CSS, like {{p { font-size: 1.25em; }}}
## Press “Submit”
# Create a work that uses the work skin
## Post > New Work
## Fill in required fields
## In the “Select work skin” field, choose the work skin you created
## Press “Post”
# Orphan the work 
## Edit > Orphan
## Select an option for keeping or removing your pseud
## Press “Yes, I’m sure”
# Log out
# Log in as orphan_account or an admin with the superadmin, support, or policy_and_abuse role
# Return to the work you just orphaned
# Follow the “Edit” link
# Change something on the form
# Press “Update”

h1. What happens

You get the error, "You do not have permission to use that work skin."

h1. What should happen

If you’re logged in as orphan_account or an admin, the {{work_skin_allowed}} validation should still let you save the work without errors and without removing the work skin.

h1. Notes

This can also affect co-creators. If your co-creator, who owns the work skin, orphans the work, you will get the "You do not have permission to use that work skin” error when trying to edit the work. 

In that case, you’ll have to remove the work skin. Allowing the use of any user’s work skin provided orphan_account is a creator of the work undermines the validation from [https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-5742|https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-5742|smart-link]. 

(I didn’t check, but I am reasonably sure this situation can also happen if your co-creator removes themselves from the work instead of orphaning the work.)

column1: Implement rich text editor for comments
column11: This is the project to use for issues related to Archive of Our Own.
column27:
We'll implement 37signals' [Lexxy|https://github.com/basecamp/lexxy/] for comments as an alternative to our HTML editor. It will work the same way as our rich text editor for works, TinyMCE, does. The editor must have toggle buttons between it and the HTML editor that also changes the help modal link to its help from HTML's, just like its work counterpart. Due to the differences in functionality described below, the content of the help file for the Lexxy-based RTE may need to differ from the help file for the TinyMCE RTE. The {{rich_text_instructions}} and {{allowed_html_instructions}} methods should be updated with an argument specifying what kind of page they're on, so we can use those same methods on all pages with editors. That argument should have three possible values: {{work}} (for forms that allow work skins, e.g. chapter), {{comment}} (for forms that are sanitized as a comment) and {{other}} (for places that are sanitized like a work but don't allow work skins, e.g. adminpost).

The style of the editor should be what Lexxy offers by default.

Unfortunately, Lexxy currently lacks some features TinyMCE has, for example alignment. For now, we might need to skip some features with similar circumstances. Another example is the image button, in Lexxy it only works for uploads, which we don't support.

It should also be a way to preview the comments you wrote, so having a text style indistinguishable to AO3's is important.

h1. Testing instructions

h4. _a. Basic editor usage_

# Find a work that allows comments, press "Comments" then "Rich Text". This is the new editor, try it!
# Use all the buttons, see if they all work as you'd expect and the comment you wrote looks exactly the same after sending it.
# The character counter should correctly indicate the characters you typed.

h4. _b. Copy and pasting things that should paste_

# Follow the instructions on [wiki.transformativeworks.org/mediawiki/Testing_the_Rich_Text_Editor|http://wiki.transformativeworks.org/mediawiki/Testing_the_Rich_Text_Editor]
# Take one of the files (preferably one that preserves all styles) and paste it in Rich Text, switch to HTML and switch back to Rich Text. Make sure it looks exactly the same as it was.
# Switch again to HTML and send the comment, it should look the same.
# Edit one of the comments you sent, switching to Rich Text should work from there too.

h4. _c. Copy and pasting things that shouldn't paste_

We don't want the editor to mislead users by showing the styles our sanitizer will sanitize later.

# Open the editor app of your choice, (e.g. Google Docs) and create a document with styles the Archive doesn't support. Included but not limited to: text color, highlighting, different fonts, indentation, image as file, line spacing.
# Paste it to the rich text editor field on a comment page and make sure that none of those styles are preserved, resulting in no changes between what editor shows after pasting and Archive shows after sending.

h4. _d. The new comment rich text help modal_

# Switch to HTML and press the question mark next to "Plain text with limited HTML".
# Switch to Rich Text and press the question mark next to "Type or paste formatted text."

The links should open a modal with some help text without any exposed HTML and without the text “translation missing”. If available, none of the links in the text in the modals should result in a 404 error.

h4. _e. Different places for commenting_

# Still on the work's page, press "Entire Work". Scroll down to the comment form and press "Rich Text". Make sure the editor works as you'd expect.
# From the page footer, change the skin to Dark Mode. Make sure the editor works as you'd expect. Repeat for all the site skins available on the footer.
# Press "Reply" on any comment on the work page. Make sure the editor works as you'd expect.
# Press "Thread", then "Reply". Make sure the editor works as you'd expect.
# Find an admin post that allows comments. Make sure the editor works as you'd expect.
# As a guest, comment on one of your works. Navigate to your account's inbox and press "Reply" to that comment. Make sure the editor works from there too.

column1: Move logic for displaying the wrangler dashboard into the show_wrangling_dashboard helper
column11: This is the project to use for issues related to Archive of Our Own.
column27:
The logic for deciding whether to display the wrangler dashboard (the sidebar shown on tag wrangling pages) is split between the {{show_wrangling_dashboard}} helper, used by the main layout, and a second, different condition wrapping the contents of the {{_wrangler_dashboard}} partial itself.

Steps to reproduce:

# Log in as a user with the tag wrangler role (see [https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/wiki/Development-Data|https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/wiki/Development-Data|smart-link] for which development account to use).
# Go to {{/tag_wranglings}}

What happens:

The wrangler dashboard is displayed in the sidebar, but the decision to display it is made in two different places with two different conditions: the layout checks {{show_wrangling_dashboard}}, and the partial then re-checks who the current user is on its first line.

What should happen:

The condition from the first line of the {{_wrangler_dashboard}} partial should move into the {{show_wrangling_dashboard}} helper, so the helper is the single place that decides whether the dashboard is displayed and the partial is only rendered when it will actually output something. The dashboard should look exactly the same before and after the change for tag wranglers (steps above) and for tag wrangling admins (log in at {{/admin/login}} as a Tag Wrangling admin, see the [https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/wiki/Development-Data|https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/wiki/Development-Data|smart-link] page), and regular users should still not see it.

The condition from the first line of the {{_wrangler_dashboard}} partial should move into the {{show_wrangling_dashboard}} helper, so the helper is the single place that decides whether the dashboard is displayed and the partial is only rendered when it will actually output something. There should be no visible changes. Specifically, on {{/tag_wranglings}}

* A user with the tag wrangler role (steps above) should see the sidebar on these pages:
** {{/tag_wranglings}}, with the links "Wrangling Home", "Wrangling Tools", "Wranglers", "Search Tags", and "New Tag", followed by a second group of links with counts: "Fandoms by media", "Characters by fandom", "Relationships by fandom", "Freeforms by fandom", and "Unsorted Tags".
** {{/unsorted_tags}}, with the same two groups of links as {{/tag_wranglings}}.
** A tag's edit page, where the second group of links shows the tag's uses (e.g. "Works", "Bookmarks", "Taggings Count") instead of the counts by category.
** {{/tag_wranglers}}, with only the first group of links.
* A Tag Wrangling admin (log in at /admin/login, see the Development Data page) should see the same sidebar on the same pages, except without the "Wrangling Home" link.
* A regular user without the tag wrangler role should not see this sidebar anywhere, and these pages should still display correctly for them.

_Hints:_ the helper is {{show_wrangling_dashboard}} in [https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/blob/master/app/helpers/tags_helper.rb#L156-L159|https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/blob/master/app/helpers/tags_helper.rb#L156-L159|smart-link]   used by the layout in [https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/blob/master/app/views/layouts/application.html.erb#L40|https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/blob/master/app/views/layouts/application.html.erb#L40|smart-link]   the partial's own condition is the first line of [https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/blob/master/app/views/tag_wranglings/_wrangler_dashboard.html.erb#L1|https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/blob/master/app/views/tag_wranglings/_wrangler_dashboard.html.erb#L1|smart-link]  . The two conditions are not identical, so the differences need to be preserved or consciously changed: the partial requires admins to have {{policy(:wrangling).read_access?}}, while the helper's {{can_wrangle?}} accepts any admin. On a tag set's Review Associations page, when there are no nominated associations to review, the page still displays a fieldset with a "Submit" button that does nothing.

Steps to reproduce:

*What happens:*

The page says "No nominated associations to review!" but still shows a fieldset with a "Submit" button below it, which does nothing.

*What should happen:*

column1: Reduce N+1 queries on series#index
column11: This is the project to use for issues related to Archive of Our Own.
column27:
h2. What happens

When a user's or pseud's series page is loaded (e.g. {{/users/*/series}}), {{SeriesController#index}} loads the series without preloading the associations the blurb needs ([series_controller.rb#L26-L40|https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/blob/master/app/controllers/series_controller.rb#L26-L40]). Rendering each series blurb then runs separate pseud and user queries per series to build the byline ([_series_module.html.erb#L20|https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/blob/master/app/views/series/_series_module.html.erb#L20]), so the number of queries grows with the number of series on the page.

h2. What should happen

Loading a user's or pseud's series page should run a constant number of queries for pseuds and users, regardless of how many series are listed. The {{Series.for_blurb}} scope already exists for this purpose ([series.rb#L61|https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/blob/master/app/models/series.rb#L61]) the index action should use it (or an equivalent {{includes}}).

Note: the fandom links in the blurb are loaded by {{Series#tag_groups}} ([series.rb#L195-L198|https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/blob/master/app/models/series.rb#L195-L198]). That method runs its own {{where}} query, so preloading does not fix it. It is out of scope for this issue. That could be a separate follow-up issue if it turns out to be worth fixing.

h2. How to see the current behavior

# Visit a user's series page, e.g. {{<http://localhost:3000/users/testuser/series}}.>
# In the Rails log (or {{log/bullet.log}}), note one pseuds/users query per series in the list instead of one for the whole page.

h2. Acceptance criteria

* Loading a user's or pseud's series page runs a constant number of queries for pseuds and users, regardless of how many series are listed.
* The blurbs still show the correct bylines (creator names link to the right pseuds/users).
* [series_n_plus_one_spec.rb|https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/blob/master/spec/requests/series_n_plus_one_spec.rb] has a {{#index}} describe asserting the query count, following the existing {{#show}} one.

h2. Hints

The same problem was fixed for {{series#show}} in [AO3-7356|https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-7356]. [PR #5668|https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/pull/5668] can serve as a model for the fix and for the request spec.

Automated test only.

column1: Disable verbose_query_logs when running tests in CI
column11: This is the project to use for issues related to Archive of Our Own.
column27:
With release [https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/projects/AO3/versions/13815/tab/release-report-all-issues|https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/projects/AO3/versions/13815/tab/release-report-all-issues|smart-link], the average run time of the controllers tests in GitHub Actions increased from 16 minutes to 22 minutes:

!before_1_8.png|width=685,alt="before_1_8.png"!

!after_1_8.png|width=712,alt="after_1_8.png"!

Local profiling around the changes made in the release shows that afterwards, a sample of controller tests (spec/controllers/admin/) spends 17% of runtime in {{ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber#log_query_source}}. This is due to {{config.active_record.verbose_query_logs}} which was enabled in the testing environment in [https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-7471|https://otwarchive.atlassian.net/browse/AO3-7471|smart-link].

By disabling the query logs only in CI where they can never be looked at, we can reduce this test runtime again, without sacrificing the [explicit request to have the logging enabled for local debugging of tests|https://github.com/otwcode/otwarchive/pull/5975#pullrequestreview-5109247143].

* 4.6% of test time is spent in {{Admin#send_set_password_notification}}, called when an admin is created, with 16% of those being created in the {{an action only authorized admins can access}} shared example
